thread.title: 2017 was the worst year yet for robocalls

author: morningstar.com
title: 2017 was the worst year yet for robocalls
text:
By Kari Paul, MarketWatch
The number of calls has increased five-fold since 2009.
Scammers have been ringing consumer phones off the hook for years, and it isn't getting better any time soon: 2017 was the worst year in history for robocalls.
There was five more times the number of robocalls in 2017 than there was in 2009, a report from the Federal Trade Comission said (https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/reports/biennial-report-congress-under-do-not-call-registry-fee-extension-act-2007-operation-national-do-not/biennial_do_not_call_report_fy_2016-2017_0.pdf). The commission received a total of 4.5 million robocall complaints in 2017, up from 3.4 million in 2016. In addition, the FTC received 2.5 million complaints about telemarketing calls, up from 1.8 million live calls.
Robocalls are the number one source of consumer complaints for the FCC, which has held contests to build better tools to block robocalls and created a "Robocall Strike Force" of major telecommunications companies to fight the calls, including AT&T (T), Apple (AAPL), Google (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Verizon (VZ).
Phone scams result in more than $350 million in financial losses annually, according to Consumers Union. Spam calls vary in purpose, according to a study released in July from caller ID and spam blocking service Truecaller (https://www.truecaller.com/), with 43% of them general nuisance, 29% scams, 19% financial service, and 7% debt collectors.
General nuisance calls are unwanted disturbance calls or pranks, spam calls are fraud attempts, financial service calls come from banks and credit unions. While many of these calls are from legitimate companies, criminals use robocall technology to collect personal information from unwitting victims.
"Robocalls are more than just a nuisance that invade our privacy at home and at work," Consumers Union wrote. "They can cost consumers real money when they are used by crooks to commit fraud, which is too often the case."
As federal organizations work on a solution, more consumers are relying on apps that block unknown numbers. Here are five:
NoMoRobo
This service was the winner of the Federal Trade Commission's 2013 Robocall Challenge, which was designed to find the best solution to robocalls and garnered nearly 800 submissions. NoMoRobo beat out the others with its blacklisting technology to intercept illegal calls. It does so by cross-checking incoming calls with its log of suspected robocallers and blocks the number after just one ring if it's a match.
If a user notices via caller ID that NoMoRobo has inadvertently blocked a wanted call, the number can be added to a whitelist for it to be allowed through the next time. NoMoRobo claims to have blocked 150 million calls since its launch in 2013 with its technology and a Consumer Reports test found 34 out of 40 testers rated it 4 out of 5 stars or above. NoMoRobo is free for landlines and $4.99 a month for mobile phones. The mobile app is compatible with Android and iOS but is currently waitlisting (https://www.nomorobo.com/beta) new customers due to high demand.
YouMail
YouMail (http://youmail.com/) plugs into a user's phone to replace traditional voice mail services and block calls. Similar to NoMoRobo, YouMail's blocker works by running numbers through its database of fraudulent callers. Unlike some other services, YouMail both blocks robocalls and prevents them from calling again by playing a dial tone to trick them into thinking the number is disconnected. Its basic services are free and work with iOS, Android, and landlines. Users can upgrade to plans with more features and the ability to handle more phones for either $5, $10, or $50 a month.
PhoneTray Pro
PhoneTray Pro is a Windows-compatible caller ID service for landlines that logs all calls and blocks telemarketers. Like YouMail, PhoneTray plays a 'number disconnected' tone to ward off repeat telemarketing calls. It also can play a federal "do not call" warning requiring telemarketers to remove you from their call list (although many have found this list is ineffective). PhoneTray Pro has a 4.5 star rating on CNET (http://download.cnet.com/PhoneTray/3000-2074_4-10540928.html) and is available for order online at a one-time charge of $29.99.
Next Caller
Backed by tech incubator Y-Combinator, this cloud-based platform runs calls through "the world's largest caller ID database" to determine if they are fraudulent. Next Caller found in a recent pilot study that the service was able to identify 98% of spoofed calls while allowing 100% of legitimate calls through its filter. It is compatible with most major landlines and starts at $99 a month. The steep price and landline-specific service caters more to large companies than individual users.
Digitone Call Blocker Plus
Digitone topped the list of landline call blockers, according to one Consumer Reports survey, with 18 out of 24 consumers who tested it saying they would purchase it. Unlike many other call blockers, it doesn't ring at all when intercepting unwanted calls. It is available for a one-time cost of $99.95 and offers a 30-day money-back guarantee.
